query: Single-phase high-entropy alloys have difficulty achieving a satisfactory strength–ductility balance. Earlier work introduced the AlCoCrFeNi2.1 eutectic high-entropy alloy with a uniform, fine lamellar structure to enable large-sized production and obtain good strength and plasticity, but its performance still falls short of industrial requirements. Its use in aircraft and spacecraft fasteners further requires stability under extreme temperature fluctuations, long-term mechanical loading, room-temperature creep, and corrosion, while relevant creep and corrosion studies remain limited by sample-size and experimental-environment constraints. Given these limitations and design requirements, what single intervention could improve the alloy’s practical performance? Present one hypothesis that specifies the intervention, causal mechanism, predicted improvement over the starting material, boundary conditions, supporting prior evidence, and a feasible experiment whose outcome could falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Adding a small amount of Zirconium (approximately 1–2 at.%) to the as-cast Al–Co–Cr–Fe–Ni eutectic high-entropy alloy will refine its lamellar interface structure by forming fine Zr-rich precipitates, thereby enhancing its strength–ductility balance, creep resistance, and corrosion stability under extreme conditions.
generation.material_initial_state: As-cast AlCoCrFeNi2.1 eutectic high-entropy alloy with a uniform, fine lamellar structure
generation.intervention: Alloying with a minor addition of Zirconium (approximately 1–2 at.%) during melt processing
generation.conditions: Sample processing remains as-cast with standard homogenization; subsequent testing under cyclic temperature fluctuations, long-term mechanical (including room-temperature creep) loading, and corrosive environments relevant to aerospace fastener applications
generation.structural_mediator: Formation of finely dispersed Zr-rich precipitates at lamellar interfaces, potentially leading to refined microstructural features that act to pin dislocations and grain boundaries
generation.mechanism: Zirconium, due to its strong affinity for certain constituent elements, is expected to precipitate as a secondary phase along the interfaces of the lamellae. These precipitates may stabilize the microstructure against coarsening under thermal cycling and enhance load-sharing across the microstructure, thereby reducing creep deformation while simultaneously improving the strength–ductility balance and resistance to corrosive degradation.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to the baseline alloy, the Zr-alloyed variant is predicted to exhibit improved mechanical performance—with increased resistance to creep and enhanced strength–ductility balance—and better corrosion resistance under the operational conditions required by aerospace applications.
generation.baseline: Performance measures of the unmodified, as-cast AlCoCrFeNi2.1 eutectic high-entropy alloy
generation.boundary: The benefits of Zirconium addition are expected to be valid for as-cast processing with limited Zr content (around 1–2 at.%); exceeding this range or altering processing parameters substantially may lead to unwanted phase formation or adverse property changes. Extreme environments beyond the tested ranges might also influence outcomes differently.
generation.uncertainty: The exact optimal Zr concentration and the long-term stability of the Zr-induced precipitates under extended cyclic temperature and mechanical loads remain uncertain due to limited systematic studies in these regimes.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two batches of the Al–Co–Cr–Fe–Ni eutectic high-entropy alloy: one control batch with the standard composition and one experimental batch with an addition of approximately 1–2 at.% Zirconium. Both batches should be produced by identical as-cast processing and homogenization conditions. Subject samples from both batches to cyclic thermal loading, long-term mechanical (creep) tests at room temperature, and corrosion tests in a relevant environment. Conduct detailed microstructural analyses (using techniques such as TEM and XRD) before and after testing.
measurements: Creep rate measurements at room temperature
Corrosion rate and pit formation analysis
Microstructural characterizations (phase identification and precipitate distribution)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the Zr-alloyed samples do not display statistically significant improvements in the strength–ductility balance, creep resistance, and corrosion behavior compared to the baseline alloy, or if adverse phases are observed that compromise the material properties, the hypothesis will be falsified.
